Injection 5 already achieved the maximum CRF; halve its gradient time to test whether full resolution can be retained in a faster method. Keeping the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed isolates the slope effect on the critical early pair.

Return to the successful 4-minute gradient and modestly increase its slope by raising phi1. This should shorten last-peak retention while testing whether the early pair retains enough of its R = 1.79 margin for full resolution.

Increase phi1 by one grid step to shorten the fully resolved method from injection 10. The early pair is close to its resolution limit at R = 1.58, so this tests the steepest acceptable gradient while holding temperature and starting composition fixed.

Return to injection 10's fully resolved gradient and raise temperature by one step to test faster elution and temperature-dependent selectivity. The critical early pair had R = 1.58, so this determines whether that margin survives modest heating.

Heating reduced early-pair resolution, so test cooling to 40 C with the faster gradient from injection 11. This should restore the critical pair above R = 1.5 while targeting a last-peak time near four minutes.

Revisit injection 9's fast gradient at lower temperature, since cooling improves the critical early-pair selectivity. This tests whether stronger cooling can recover full resolution while keeping the last peak earlier than the best fully resolved 4-minute gradient.

Raise phi1 one step to accelerate the last peak, which eluted during the hold in injection 14. The critical early pair has R = 1.72, providing some margin for the modest increase in gradient steepness.
Raise phi1 one more grid step to shorten the last peak's hold-phase retention. The early pair at R = 1.60 is near the limit, so this tests whether further acceleration preserves full resolution.

Raise phi0 one step to narrow the gradient window and reduce its slope, testing whether the early pair recovers the small resolution deficit from injection 16. This also targets faster final-peak elution, while checking that the higher starting organic fraction does not compromise early retention.

Shift both endpoints upward one step, preserving injection 17's successful gradient slope while accelerating the last peak. This tests whether the early pair remains sufficiently retained and resolved at the higher starting organic fraction.

Raise phi0 one grid step to narrow the gradient and seek a shorter fully resolved run. Injection 18's early pair has R = 1.64; this tests whether the shallower slope offsets the loss of initial retention.
Raise temperature one step from injection 19 to shorten final-peak retention while testing its early-pair resolution margin of R = 1.77. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate the temperature effect.

Increase temperature one more grid step to test the fastest fully resolved temperature at this gradient. The early pair has only a small margin at R = 1.58, so this run will establish whether further heating sacrifices the maximum CRF.

Return to 25 C to recover early-pair selectivity, then raise phi0 one step to test a narrower, faster gradient window. This probes the starting-composition limit, with early-peak under-retention now the main risk.

Test a lower-starting-organic alternative to injection 20 while preserving its gradient slope and temperature. This should retain the early peaks more strongly and targets another fully resolved, sub-three-minute separation; injection 20 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Reduce phi1 one step from injection 20 to gain early-pair resolution margin while retaining a short run. This tests a less steep alternative expected to preserve maximum CRF, with injection 20 retained as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Cool injection 24 by one step to increase the critical early-pair resolution margin while keeping a short, fully resolved separation. The maximum CRF is already achieved; this final run tests a more tolerant alternative to injection 20, the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.
